I'm very much liking the set up of Charlotte so far, both from a raw production quality standpoint and for potential it has to take us places. As someone else mentioned in another discussion, the powers seem to be highly linked to some sort of personal trauma during adolescence. Glasses-kun can go infinitely fast, but doesn't have the power to control where he's going - much like how a lot of kids have crazy potential for a lot of things but can't manage to focus their energies on a specific goal. Nao can turn invisible to one specific person... which would be a pretty handy power if you happened to be in an abusive family situation. Yuu can control others, when his (brief) story flashbacks seem to indicate he's been in a family situation in which he's had no control of his situation (disappeared dad, absent mom, etc). Plus, the powers "phase out" in time, which would be analogous to a teenager overcoming whatever trauma it was that led them to developing the powers - much in the same way that teens tend to get over past conflicts as part of growing up normally.

Whether the symbolism is intentional or not remains to be seen, but if it is a dedicated theme I'm excited to see where they're taking it.

I enjoy field work and have rock descriptions etc down to a tee, but my sketches pretty much universally suck. Any ideas or resources you know of would be hugely appreciated.

Sketching doesn't come naturally to most of us, so I think the best way to improve is just by practice. I was rubbish at it too, and then I took a course where every single lab class we had to do 4-5 sketches, and just doing it every week had me improving drastically. I'm not that convinced by how good they need to be anyway really, in my mind the importance of a sketch is that it forces you to pay attention to detail and remember features of the outcrop just by doing it, and that's much more use than the actual sketch will be in future. That's my 2 cents, anyhow!
Thanks! It seems the take-home message is practise, practise, practise!

It may not really apply here, but the best advice I have gotten about drawing physical objects is to forget that they are what they are. For example, if you are drawing a geometric/roughly cubic rock, image it is a surface, with, say 9 vertices. From there, connect the vertices as if it were some "alien object" that you have never seen before. That way, you won't make assumptions in what it looks like; you will draw what it actually IS - not what you believe it to be.

One of the things that's helped me the most was some advice from a professor: start with the big things, then add in detail. For example if I was trying to sketch a road cut with 4 members first I would sketch the overall shape of the entire road cut (rectangular, at an angle, anticlinal, etc), second I would try to sketch the contacts of the rock members in the road cut, then move down and sketch features of the individual members (cross bedding, folds, foliation, bed thickness, etc). Just remember that they are FIELD sketches, no one expects them to be museum quality. Like Prunesquallor said, it forces you to pay attention to the outcrop and can also help jog your memory if you come back to it in your notebook later on. I had a hell of a time with the "Rite in the Rain" field books, I could never erase anything and the page layout kept boxing me in, what I ended up doing was getting a different, non-waterproof notebook and a gallon ziplock bag because that worked better for me. Do what works for you, I've even done sketches in a little artist's sketchbook and then taped or glued the pages into my field book later. Good luck!
Thanks for the advice! It seems that I need to take a different approach then, I would do the try to draw everything at once kinda tactic

That was my biggest challenge to overcome as well, I tried to draw finished quality pictures right off the bat. After talking with some artist friends and taking a couple of classes I found out that's basically the worst way to draw and even professional artists don't usually work that way. The process that is most common among artists (as far as I'm aware): Draw the simple shape that most closely matches (a circle for someone's head as example), then refine that circle into more of an egg shape, then layout lines where the facial features would go (horizontal line about 2/3 up for the eyes, vertical line halfway for nose, middle of mouth etc), then start drawing basic shape of features (ovals for eyes, blocky shapes for nose), then refine the features. There is a ton of erasing to a good drawing and another required skill for sketching is to draw lightly so when you erase your layout lines they are gone completely. The advantage of sketching that way is that it's easier to have the correct spatial relationships between subjects instead of spending all your time drawing a finished section with tons of detail and then attempting to connect it to another subject you haven't even started on yet.
